5.key: Unresolved. MuseScore's news analysis gives C# minor: the melody is moved down a half step from the 'I Follow Rivers' original in D minor, and the chorus is harmonized C#m-G#m-E-G#m. Karaoke-version lists G# minor. That chord loop has no A or A#, so the harmony fits either tonal center, and the two sources may be hearing the same loop differently.
5.style_basis: Wikipedia (as summarized) calls it a melodic hip-hop song. Songfacts describes a split personality: a soft-focus R&B love song set against a blistering indictment, over a beat with a dark atmosphere and a hypnotic synth line. Karaoke-version describes a dark synth figure and snapping drums. No source describes 808 or hi-hat programming. The 'trap' half of the tag only maps 'melodic hip-hop' onto this taxonomy and is not a verified description of the drums. 'rnb_rap' would also be defensible.
5.opening_detail: No cited source describes the first seconds of the record: instrumental intro, producer tag, ad-lib, or chorus. Karaoke-version describes the overall palette (dark synth figure, snapping drums, a chorus that loops like a taunt) but not the intro. The search summary says Variety quotes an 'opening line' about his work and death. That might mean the first vocal is a verse line rather than the chorus, but it is not clear the quote is the song's first line, so the opening is left unknown.
5.producer_tag_detail: No source mentions a producer tag (FnZ, Rogét Chahayed or b4u) on the record.
5.hook_description: The chorus interpolates the melodic hook of Lykke Li's 2011 single 'I Follow Rivers' (the 'I follow you' hook) under new Drake lyrics. Songfacts, Complex and Billboard Canada all call it an interpolation: a re-sung melody, not a sampled recording. MuseScore says the melody is transposed down a half step (D minor to C# minor) and set over C#m-G#m-E-G#m. Search-summarized coverage also says the melody is slowed down; that claim most likely comes from MuseScore or Yardbarker, but which one was not confirmed. Karaoke-version calls it a 'clipped, Auto-Tuned hook' and says the chorus 'loops like a taunt'. HotNewHipHop says the hook slides through different pitches and calls it the chorus that instantly sticks. Complex calls it 'almost impossibly catchy' and says its melodic peculiarity comes from 'I Follow Rivers'. Stereogum calls the track an undeniable hit built from a 'flipped, pitch-shifted' Lykke Li hit. Songfacts says the vocals use formant bending, beyond standard Auto-Tune. The beat's producer, Rogét Chahayed, reportedly did not notice the interpolation until fans pointed it out online. That means the recognizable melody lives in Drake's topline, not in the beat.
5.beat_switch_detail: No source describes a beat switch in this song. The only ICEMAN beat switch the reviews mention is on '2 Hard 4 the Radio' (The Line of Best Fit), where the beat switches to a West Coast style. Songfacts' 'split-personality' framing (a soft R&B love song against attacks on gossip culture, with the verses shifting into aggression) describes a split in lyrics and tone, not a documented production change. Absence of a switch is not confirmed either.

delivery_observations.observation: The chorus is sung through Auto-Tune rather than rapped: it re-sings the 'I Follow Rivers' melody with Drake's own lyrics. HotNewHipHop says the hook slides through different pitches and credits these 'vocal shifts' for its stickiness.

Karaoke-version's listing calls the hook 'clipped' and Auto-Tuned and says the chorus 'loops like a taunt'. That wording suggests short, repeated phrases rather than a long melodic line, but this is my reading of the listing; it gives no bar positions.
Vocal processing is the signature. Songfacts says this is the most extreme vocal processing on ICEMAN: it goes past standard Auto-Tune into formant bending, which makes his timbre deeper and warped.

A small blog review says the vocal effects run through the whole song and give his voice a 'processed, layered quality' without pulling focus from the performance. It does not say whether the layering is doubles, harmonies or effects. Low-authority source.

The tone changes between sections. Songfacts frames the record as a soft-focus R&B love song set against a blistering indictment of internet gossip culture, industry enemies and the noise around his public life, and says the verses shift into aggression aimed at gossip culture, critics, industry figures and rivals. No source describes the verse cadence, syllable density or pocket.

5.most_audible_change: No source found documents what changes when a section returns. The only contrast the sources describe is between two sections. The chorus is the Lykke Li-derived sung melody, heavily processed (formant-bent and Auto-Tuned, sliding in pitch, 'clipped', looping). The verses, per Songfacts, turn aggressive in content and tone. Nothing found describes drum, 808, dropout, double or ad-lib changes on any return.
5.return_anchor: The interpolated 'I Follow Rivers' chorus melody. Sources agree it is what sticks: Complex calls it 'almost impossibly catchy', HotNewHipHop calls it the chorus that instantly sticks, and karaoke-version says it 'loops like a taunt'. It is an original topline that re-sings a widely known melody, moved down a half step, reportedly slowed, and heavily processed, over an original beat (dark synth line, snapping drums) whose makers did not know the interpolation was there. Lykke Li reportedly approved the use.

samples.work: Lykke Li - 'I Follow Rivers' (2011, from Wounded Rhymes)
samples.how_used: Interpolation, not a sample of the recording: the chorus melody is re-sung with new Drake lyrics. MuseScore says it is transposed down a half step (D minor to C# minor) and harmonized C#m-G#m-E-G#m. Search-summarized coverage says the melody is slowed down. It is delivered clipped, Auto-Tuned and formant-processed. Karaoke-version lists Lykke Li and Björn Yttling among the credited writers. A lawsuit by songwriter Aviel Hirschfield alleges the chorus is essentially identical to the chorus of his own demo, which also interpolated 'I Follow Rivers'; Drake's camp denies this. Drake previously used Lykke Li's 'Little Bit' on So Far Gone (2009).

5.context_note: Chart: it debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 dated 2026-05-30, with 40.7M official streams for the tracking week ending May 21. It was Drake's 14th No. 1, the most for a male soloist, breaking his tie with Michael Jackson, and his first multi-week No. 1 of the decade. It went to US rhythmic radio on May 19, 2026 with 56 adds. History: Songfacts says Drake previewed it on the 'Iceman: Episode 3' livestream (September 4, 2025) as 'That's Just How I Feel', then reworked and retitled it. HotNewHipHop reports Drake said he made 'Janice STFU' three days before ICEMAN dropped. Beat origin, per a partial excerpt of the Billboard Canada interview: it came from a late-March jam with FnZ at Chahayed's home studio. The same excerpt quotes Chahayed about an earlier beat made with London Cyr that had 'cool synth horns', but it is not fully confirmed that this refers to this beat. Songfacts says b4u added finishing touches before the beat went to OVO. Reportedly, Chahayed first heard the final song on the livestream and only noticed the interpolation when fans pointed it out; the search summary did not pin whether that comes from Songfacts or Billboard Canada. Studio takeaway, using only what the sources support: the part listeners recognize is a topline built by re-singing a familiar melody, transposed, reportedly slowed, and made strange with formant and Auto-Tune processing, over an original dark synth and snap beat. Tempo, feel and structure could not be verified, and the web-search budget ran out before the livestream-versus-album version differences could be checked.

The 167.1 grid is that value doubled, following the half-time trap convention. The rap-bar pulse is about 83.5, which fits the runtime and the long verses (about 67 felt bars in 192 s). No source describes the feel in pulse terms.
53.opening_detail: Wikipedia says the track opens with a spoken-word intro. The Duke Chronicle says a single piano key sets off the intro, and the 'shark' build leads up to a later beat drop. AOL describes a menacing piano before the bass-heavy trap beat hits as she takes her first shots. So the first thing a listener hears is sparse, ominous piano with Megan speaking, not rapping and not singing a hook. The full drums arrive with the first rapped shots. No source says whether the first piano note comes before her first spoken word, and none gives timings.
53.producer_tag_detail: None of the sources found mention a producer tag (for example a LilJuMadeDaBeat tag) on the track.
53.hook_description: There is no conventional chorus. Lyreka (an interpretive song-meaning site, so a weak source) says 'There's no traditional chorus' and describes the verse as 'a series of clean strikes.' Wikipedia's structure description fits this: a spoken-word intro, verse 1, a spoken-word break, then verse 2, with no chorus mentioned. The song opens on spoken word over piano, not on a hook.
53.return_anchor: With no chorus, three things give the listener something to come back to. (1) The piano line: LilJuMadeDaBeat says it was the first element he built and that it runs through the whole song (Complex). (2) The two spoken-word passages, the intro and the break between the verses, which mark the structure (Wikipedia). (3) Quotable one-off punchlines, such as the widely reported 'Megan's Law' line (AOL). These do the memorability work a refrain normally does; none of them is a repeated chant.

delivery_observations.observation: The rap starts with the drums. After a menacing piano intro, the bass-heavy trap beat hits as she takes her first shots, so the first rapped bars are also the first full-beat bars.

Reviewers single out her flow switches. ACRN says she 'switches it up at exactly the right moments' to give the song a sense of progress, which matters on a song with no chorus. Modern Music Analysis credits 'aggressive delivery and several flow switches' with making the disses land as final.

She leaves rap cadence twice for spoken word: the intro and a spoken break between verse 1 and verse 2. Reviews describe these as direct address to her critics. They reset the energy before the next rapped section.

A user review on Musicboard (a weak source) calls the rapid-fire delivery the track's standout element. Wikipedia describes the delivery as aggressive and confident and notes critical praise for the flow.

The vocal came before the beat. Megan wrote the first verse, and recorded about half or all of it, over a different beat. She sent LilJuMadeDaBeat the a cappella, and he built the instrumental around it, starting with the piano line. The flow was set first and the beat was fitted to it. He also says he did not think the beat was remarkable when he made it.

53.beat_switch_detail: No source reports a beat switch. LilJuMadeDaBeat says the piano line runs through the whole song, which fits one continuous instrumental. The 'switches' reviewers praise are Megan's flow switches, not a new beat. The one arrangement event the sources describe is the drum drop after the spoken piano intro. The 'no' is from recollection, not a source.

Between the verses the rap stops for a spoken-word break, dropping from dense rap to speech before verse 2 starts. No source says whether the beat drops out under this break.

The melodic layer stays the same. The piano line runs through the song (LilJuMadeDaBeat), so contrast between sections comes from the drum entrance, the spoken passages and Megan's flow switches, not from new melodic material.

53.most_audible_change: The drum and 808 drop after the spoken piano intro: the menacing piano gives way to a bass-heavy trap beat as she starts rapping. After that there is no chorus return and no beat switch. The contrasts that matter are the mid-song spoken break and her flow switches within the verses (ACRN: she 'switches it up at exactly the right moments').

53.context_note: Studio summary: this is a hookless diss-track layout. Ominous piano with spoken word, then the drums drop on the first rapped bars, a long verse driven by flow switches, a spoken-word reset, and a second verse. The verse was written and partly recorded before this beat existed, and the instrumental was built around the a cappella, starting from the piano line (Complex interview with LilJuMadeDaBeat). It debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 (chart dated 2024-02-10), her first No. 1 as a solo artist. Reception praised the lyrics and flow, and the perceived disses (for example the 'Megan's Law' line) drove much of the attention. Billboard's Iceman ranking says Future opening the song was a strong call and that Drake 'didn't make them wait' for the reunion, so the first thing a listener recognizes is Future's voice and the Drake-Future reunion. Low-authority lyric-interpretation pages describe the opening as street-heavy bars ('raw street talk') before Drake takes over. That is why this is tagged rap_verse rather than hook. Two low-authority lyric-interpretation pages mention a hook: Driftzine refers to a Drake 'hook' that frames Atlanta as proof of his reach, and another page refers to Future 'chorus-style sections'. No review, credits page or Genius section breakdown confirms a conventional chorus, who sings it, where it first appears or how often it returns. It is also unconfirmed whether the title phrase works as the hook. What sources do confirm as memorable anchors: (1) Future opening the song, the reunion moment (Billboard); (2) the beat switch into a murkier second beat, with Future's showcase verse after it, the structural pivot familiar from 'Life Is Good' and 'N 2 Deep' (Songfacts, Billboard); (3) Molly Santana's verse, built around a repeated Hannah Montana comparison (Wikipedia), which one write-up calls slogan-like and built on repetition and self-naming.
6.return_anchor: The beat switch is the sourced landmark, the 'Part II' pivot. The track leaves its first, rage-style beat for a murkier, more anxious second beat, and Future comes back for a 'vintage beat-switch performance' (Songfacts; Billboard). Inside Part II, Molly Santana's repeated Hannah Montana comparison is a second repeated anchor (Wikipedia). A recurring title-phrase chorus is not confirmed by any authoritative source.

6.beat_switch_detail:
- Songfacts: Future's verse comes after a beat switch that pushes the production into 'murkier, more anxious' territory, a structural pivot it compares to the Drake/Future songs 'N 2 Deep' and 'Life Is Good'.
- Billboard (Iceman track ranking): later in the song Drake gives Future 'the vintage beat-switch performance' in the style of their earlier hits.
- Stay Free Radio: frames the song as Part I / Part II. Part II 'flips into full luxury mode' and contains Molly Santana's verse.
- An Album of the Year listener review confirms two distinct beats; the reviewer wished there were no switch, though both beats are 'cool'.
- IMAMusicMogul blog (non-authoritative, uncorroborated): Beat 1 at 145 BPM in F minor, Beat 2 at 135 BPM in Eb minor. If true, the switch also drops the tempo.
No source gives a timestamp for the switch.

delivery_observations.observation: The performance is split across two beats. Future opens on beat 1, Drake takes over, and after the switch Future returns for what Billboard calls a 'vintage beat-switch performance' in the mold of earlier Drake/Future collaborations. The post-switch half is a new showcase for a different rapper, not a repeat of the first half's pattern. Songfacts draws the same parallel to 'Life Is Good' and 'N 2 Deep'.

Molly Santana's verse is built around a repeated comparison to Hannah Montana (Wikipedia). One interpretive write-up describes her verse as more direct and slogan-like than the others, built on repetition and self-naming. Her device is a recurring phrase she keeps returning to, not dense multisyllabic rhyme.

Dazed (Solomon Pace-McCarrick) names Future's and Molly Santana's performances as clear highlights that suit the maximalist rage beat (distorted melodies, neon-lit synths, 808s). This is evaluative only; it gives no technical detail on where their phrases or rhymes land.

audit.notes:
None of the pre-tagged non-rap songs I checked turned out to be classified as rap by Billboard, so the flagged list is empty. I used all 8 searches and never got a budget-exhausted notice.

What the evidence codes mean:
- E1: The song is on Billboard's Hot R&B Songs chart, which never shares a song with Hot Rap Songs, so it is not rap.
- E2: Rap drought. The Source (2026-04-10), HotNewHipHop and Complex all reported that no hip-hop song reached the Hot 100 top 10 between Drake's 'What Did I Miss?' (debuted at No. 2 in July 2025) and April 2026, about nine months. Separately, Billboard reported that the charts dated 2025-10-25 and 2025-11-01 had no rap songs in the top 40, the first time since 1990. Any song in the top 10 during that window was therefore not counted as rap.
- E3: The Year-End 2021 Hot Rap Songs list (Wikipedia, citing Billboard) runs 1. Mood, 2. Astronaut in the Ocean, 3. Up, 4. Industry Baby, 5. Rapstar. A song that earned more points over the year and was on Hot Rap Songs would rank above these, so its absence means it was never on that chart.
- E4: The same test using the Year-End 2022 Hot Rap Songs top 16 (1. First Class, 2. Wait for U, 3. Big Energy ... 16. Puffin on Zootiez). Bruno, Me Porto Bonito, Titi Me Pregunto and About Damn Time are all missing even though they ranked higher on the 2022 Year-End Hot 100. Those Hot 100 year-end ranks come from my memory; the Hot Rap Songs list comes from the search.
- E5: Dracula reached the top 10 on 2026-05-16. That is after the April 2026 drought reports and before Drake's ICEMAN filled the top 10 (NPR, 2026-05-28: nine of the top 10, led by 'Janice STFU' at No. 1). I found no rap-chart listing for it. I did not confirm which song first ended the drought or on what date, so this classification is inferred, not proven. Be Her (2026-04-18), Drop Dead (2026-05-02), Doors and I Can't Love You Anymore (2026-05-09) fall in the same window and are plainly non-rap. I did not list them as checked.

Not conclusively checked, and I don't believe any is rap:
- Fancy Like (Walker Hayes): country song with a rap-style delivery. From memory, Billboard filed it on Hot Country Songs. Its absence from the 2021 Year-End Hot Rap top 5 doesn't settle it because its yearly points were lower.
- Permission To Dance and My Universe (BTS): the 2021 Year-End top 5 doesn't settle these either.
- Fortnight, I Had Some Help and I Ain't Coming Back: Post Malone is credited, but these are pop/country. From memory, I Had Some Help was on Hot Country Songs.
- 2023 Latin songs (Monaco, Where She Goes, Un x100to, TQG, Bzrp Vol. 53, Ella Baila Sola) and Bad Bunny's 2025 songs: not searched, plainly Latin.
- Everything from June to October 2026 (after ICEMAN) and all the other plainly pop, country, R&B and holiday entries: not searched, as the task instructed.

Stated Hot 100 ranks: none were confirmed directly. Two consistent data points: About Damn Time debuted at No. 50 on 2022-04-30 and later reached No. 1, and 'What Did I Miss?' debuted at No. 2 in July 2025.

yearend.notes:
All five Hot Rap Songs year-end lists came from the Wikipedia 'Billboard Year-End Hot Rap Songs of <year>' pages, which cite Billboard's year-end issues. For 2025 the top 10 was also checked against Billboard's own list article (billboard.com/lists/kendrick-lamar-sza-rap-songs-year-end-charts-top-10/), and the two agree. None of the lists is complete. The search tool's page extraction stops at about 27 rows.

WHAT IS COVERED
- 2021 (25 positions): ranks 1-18, 20 and 25. Missing: 19 and 21-24. One summary said 26 entries, which is probably a counting artifact.
- 2022 (50 positions): ranks 1-23 and 30. Missing: 24-29 and 31-50. The artist for #23 'F.N.F.' was cut off. Hitkidd & GloRilla is from memory only.
- 2023 (50 positions): ranks 1-27 and 50. Missing: 28-49. The artist for #23 'On BS' comes from a Spotify playlist. A Sporcle quiz orders ranks 22-24 differently. An Uproxx excerpt put 'Rich Flex' at No. 14 on an unclear chart; Wikipedia, citing Billboard, has it at No. 1, so No. 1 is used. #18 was extracted as 'Put It on da Floor'; the Billboard title is believed (from memory) to be 'Put It on da Floor Again'.
- 2024 (50 positions): ranks 1-27. Missing: 28-50. The artist for #5 was missing from the 2024 text; it is Doja Cat on the 2023 list.
- 2025: ranks 1-14. The Wikipedia extract stops at #14, and the list length is unknown. For #9 the artist is spelled 'AzChike' on Wikipedia and 'AzChiki' in the Billboard write-up.

TRACKS ON MORE THAN ONE LIST (all rap): Industry Baby and Way 2 Sexy (2021, 2022); Vegas and Super Freaky Girl (2022, 2023); Paint the Town Red and FukUMean (2023, 2024); Not Like Us (2024, 2025).

BORDERLINE TRACKS CONFIRMED AS RAP by these lists: Drake's 'Sticky' (2022 #19), 'Search & Rescue' (2023 #8), 'Superhero (Heroes & Villains)' with Chris Brown (2023 #7), 'Rich Baby Daddy' featuring SZA (2024 #11), Bryson Tiller's 'Whatever She Wants' (2024 #17), Paul Russell's 'Lil Boo Thang' (2024 #15), 'Sweetest Pie' with Dua Lipa (2022 #10), 'To the Moon' by Jnr Choi (2022 #18), Doja Cat's 'Paint the Town Red' and 'Agora Hills', Kendrick Lamar & SZA's 'Luther' (2025 #1), and Carti & The Weeknd's 'Rather Lie' (2025 #11).

HOT R&B SONGS YEAR-END LISTS: no rows found. The 2023, 2024 and 2025 searches returned only weekly Hot R&B Songs pages; the year-end pages did not appear. 2021 and 2022 were not searched because the budget went to the rap lists, as the task asked.

Side evidence from weekly charts (not year-end rows):
- 'Timeless' (The Weeknd & Playboi Carti) is listed on the Wikipedia/Wikiwand Hot R&B Songs article among the songs with the most weeks at No. 1 (2024-25), so it is R&B, not rap. Source: wikiwand.com/en/articles/R&B_Songs.
- Tyla's 'Water' was No. 2 (peak 2) on Hot R&B Songs dated 2023-12-23, so it is R&B. Source: billboard.com/charts/r-and-b-songs/2023-12-23/.
- Chris Brown's 'Summer Too Hot' and Coco Jones' 'ICU' were on Hot R&B Songs in 2023.
- 'Gas Station Love' by EJ Jones x BigXthaPlug was on Hot R&B Songs in December 2025.
- Billboard also has a list titled 'SZA & Kendrick Lamar Are All Over the Year-End R&B/Hip-Hop Charts' (billboard.com/lists/kendrick-lamar-sza-rb-hip-hop-year-end-charts-top-10/). Its contents were not retrieved.

INFERENCE, NOT EVIDENCE: 'Creepin'' (Metro Boomin, The Weeknd & 21 Savage) is absent from the 2023 rap ranks 1-27. From memory only, it was a top-5 year-end Hot 100 song of 2023, so its absence suggests it is not on Hot Rap Songs. Treat this as low confidence until a Hot R&B Songs page confirms it.

UNRESOLVED: tracks not found in the rows above may sit in the missing ranks, so their absence proves nothing. This includes FE!N, Slime You Out, Boy's a Liar Pt. 2, Kill Bill, Snooze, Saturn, 30 for 30, What Did I Miss?, Evil J0rdan, Wacced Out Murals, Reincarnated, Hiss, Family Matters, and Falling Back.

Hot 100 ranks were not confirmed in these searches.

All 14 searches were used: 7 standard and 7 extended.

Billboard describes the hook as viral and X-rated. The song was the first No. 1 for Rich the Kid and Playboi Carti.

38.title: Houdini
38.hook_device: Interpolation of the Steve Miller Band's 'Abracadabra' chorus, with the beat also built on that sample

notable.claim: The song begins with singsong rhymes that call back to his 2002 single 'Without Me'. This is a separate intro, not the 'Abracadabra' chorus.
Eminem and Luis Resto built the beat and chorus on a sample of the Steve Miller Band's 1982 'Abracadabra', and the chorus interpolates it.
Songfacts: the word 'Houdini' doesn't appear until 736 words into the song.
It also interpolates earlier Eminem songs, including 'Without Me' and 'My Name Is'.

8.title: Shabang
8.hook_device: Drake's shout-out to the producer ('Maneesh on the beat'), used as the chorus. This is disputed: one review says the closest thing to a chorus is a repeated, self-soothing chant.

notable.claim: Produced by Toronto producer Maneesh, co-produced by 40 (Noah Shebib).
The track opens with Drake's shout-out to the producer. Maneesh says he first took the line as a shout-out, then realized at release that it is the chorus.
MyBesh disagrees: it says the closest the song comes to a chorus is a repeated, self-soothing chant, not a hook.
Another review describes sped-up vocals and a bright R&B feel before the punchy beat drops, which conflicts with the shout-out-first description. The summary did not name the review.
In a viral 'Shabang' challenge, fans edit objects appearing out of thin air during the hook.
